Memory That Follows the Tree: Git-Tracked ASN Ledgers and Tiered Aggregation in ASL

2026-09-08Architecture & Memory Systems6 min read

These notes were written in September 2026, before the C host was removed, and describe designs as well as shipped behaviour. Where a post says asl-host check or asl-host test, the command today is asl check or asl test; ERR_READ_UNBALANCED is now ERR_UNBALANCED; and the current checker does not reject an unmarked effect (ERR_EFFECT_UNMARKED). Figures are the ones measured on the date each post gives. Current docs

By GenSEAM | September 2026

In AgentSlang (ASL), agent memory lives in the repository as typed ASN S-expression ledgers—the same notation used for code and tool calls—queried on demand instead of dumped wholesale into every prompt. Decisions, audits and architectural invariants sit in git alongside the modules they govern, so a reviewer or another agent can inspect them with one query.

Most agent harnesses start with the opposite habit: a flat context dump. Whenever an agent needs orientation, tooling pours whole files (cat, view_file) or loose Markdown notes into one buffer. As a codebase grows into dozens of packages, that flat buffer breaks down:

  1. Context contamination: unrelated source files crowd out working memory and invite hallucinations.
  2. Attention dilution: constraints buried mid-prompt are easy for a model to miss.
  3. Repeated cost: every reasoning step pays to re-read the same structural facts.

Even a binary "global vs. local" split is too blunt for a tree of subsystems, packages and modules. This post describes the git-tracked ledger memory we run today in ASL, and the recursive, tree-aggregated design we are building on top of it.

1. Today: Plain Ledgers, One Directory

Our memory is plain ASN text in a memory directory at the workspace root, kept beside the code it describes. The tools know a handful of ledger kinds:

  • intent and roadmap ledgers: what the work is for and what comes next.
  • a decisions ledger: decision records with their rationale.
  • a notes ledger: observations, written and listed with the (:note) op.

The ops that touch it are confined to it. (:mem :op list|get|query|put ...) reads and stages row-keyed ledger changes, and a path that leaves that directory is rejected with ERR_BOUNDARY_VIOLATION. (:note :action :list) reports the notes ledger, and asl '(:observe :dim memory)' reports ledger sizes; the old asl mem command is retired in its favour.

The ledgers are workspace state, not part of the published language repository: a fresh clone of it has no memory directory, and (:note :action :list) there answers :status :empty. Today there is one tier, the workspace that holds the working directory.

2. The Target: Self-Similar Tiers at Depth N

The design we are building extends that one directory into a recursion:

Tier 0 workspace -> Tier 1 subsystems -> Tier 2 packages -> Tier 3 components -> Tier 4 modules
Workspace memory directory
├── Subsystem: asl
│   ├── Package: asl-checker
│   └── Package: asl-compiler
│       └── Component: codegen
└── Subsystem: agent-bus

Three properties define it:

  1. Self-similarity: every node uses the same memory schema (intent, decisions, invariants, knowledge), so a tool that reads one tier reads them all.
  2. Local ownership: a decision made inside a package is recorded in that package's memory and reaches the root only when an upper tier aggregates it.
  3. Inheritance: a child tier inherits its parent's constraints unless it records an explicit, reasoned override.

Only the root tier exists today; ledgers below it are the next step.

3. Memory as Code

In most systems memory is passive text: Markdown, JSON, or embeddings. An agent reads it, translates it, and writes glue to apply it.

In ASL, memory records are S-expressions, the same syntax as the code, and a function is a value that a record can hold. An invariant can therefore carry its own check. This runs today:

(module probe/invariant :x [Invariant noDoubleComment zeroComment holds runTests])

schema Invariant
  id: String
  scope: String
  predicate: (Fn [String] -> Bool)

fn noDoubleComment source: String -> Bool
  (not (stringContains? source ";;"))

fn zeroComment -> Invariant
  {:id "C0001" :scope "asl/packages/asl-checker" :predicate noDoubleComment}

fn holds inv: Invariant source: String -> Bool
  (let [(p inv.predicate)] (p source))

fn runTests -> Bool
  (do
    (assert (holds (zeroComment) "(+ 1 2)") "clean source holds")
    (refute (holds (zeroComment) ";; note") "commented source fails")
    true)

asl test on this file prints 1 assertion(s) executed, 1 refutation(s) executed (2 passed) (2026-10-14). Today our ledgers hold data, not predicates; storing executable invariants in the memory directory so that a gate can evaluate them directly is part of the design.

4. Logical Addresses (Target)

Physical paths are host-specific: they change when a package moves or runs inside a browser's virtual file system. The design adds logical memory addresses resolved by a small resolver:

  • mem:root/intent: the workspace intent.
  • mem:asl/checker/invariants: the checker package's invariants.

The resolver would look in an in-memory cache first and hydrate from the tier's memory files on a miss, so the agent names what it wants and the storage can be the local disk, a Git snapshot, or a browser file system. None of this is implemented yet; today tools address memory by workspace-relative path.

5. Aggregation (Target)

Focused work wants local memory; coordinators and humans also want the whole picture. The aggregation we are building walks every tier and emits one compact ASN stream, for example:

(:memorySnapshot
  :tiers 2
  :subsystems [
    (:subsystem :name "asl" :path "asl" :memory "asl/<memory directory>")
  ]
  :status :consistent)

The shape above is illustrative; no command produces it yet. When it ships it will be an agent-plane op listed by asl '(:tools)'.

An earlier version of this post printed a tree and a comparison table (token cost per turn, pollution rate, scan time, pass rate) for flat, two-tier and fractal memory. No run backs those figures, so we removed them. We will publish a comparison when it comes from a recorded run with its method, scope and date.

6. Conclusion

Memory for an agent is not a key-value store or a pile of notes. It is the structure through which the agent sees the system. Our current memory is deliberately plain: line-oriented ASN ledgers in one directory beside the code. The recursion, the logical addresses and the aggregation are where it is going, and each will be described as shipped only when a command does it.
